note: 50 questions, all foundational. Each one aims to land a genuine surprise while staying guessable — answer options use clear magnitude ladders or a plain contrast between what you'd assume and what's true. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research. whyWrong is index-aligned with options; null at the correct index.

questions.prompt: Over the last 30 years, has the number of people in extreme poverty gone up or down?
questions.whyCorrect: About 1.5 billion people escaped extreme poverty since 1990 — one of the biggest improvements in human history. Most adults guess the opposite.
whyWrong: It fell from about 2.3 billion people to about 800 million — an enormous change.
This is the most common wrong guess in the world. Poverty fell dramatically.
questions.action: Ask three adults to guess. Most will get it wrong.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many people leave extreme poverty every single day?
questions.whyCorrect: About 118,000 people a day, averaged over 35 years. It never makes the news because 'things got slightly better again today' isn't a headline.
whyWrong: A thousand times too small to add up to 1.5 billion people.
Still far too small — that would take 4,000 years.
questions.action: Notice which kinds of news get reported, and which don't.

questions.prompt: How much money a day marks the line for extreme poverty?
questions.whyCorrect: Just $3.00 a day — and that has to cover everything. Food, shelter, clothes, heat. Not spending money left over; the whole lot.
whyWrong: A hundred times too high — almost nobody on Earth is above that.
Ten times too high. About 81% of the world lives below $30 a day.
questions.action: Add up what you spent yesterday and compare.

questions.prompt: In 1820, roughly what share of the world lived in extreme poverty?
questions.whyCorrect: Three-quarters of everyone alive. For most of human history, being poor was normal — a comfortable life for most people is a very recent invention.
whyWrong: That's today's figure, two centuries later.
The world didn't get down to half until 1956.
questions.action: Ask what your town was like 200 years ago.

questions.prompt: When did less than half the world live in extreme poverty for the first time?
questions.whyCorrect: 1956 — within living memory for some people's grandparents. For all of history before that, most humans alive were extremely poor.
whyWrong: Poverty was near-universal then.
Still around three-quarters in 1820.
questions.action: Work out how old someone born in 1956 is now.

questions.prompt: Where do most of the world's poor people live?
questions.whyCorrect: About 65% of the world's poor — 740 million people — live in middle-income countries. A country's average can rise while millions inside it are left behind.
whyWrong: A very common assumption. The poorest countries have the highest *rates*, but smaller populations.
Rich countries have poverty, but not most of the world's.
questions.action: Look up your country's average income, then who lives below it.

questions.prompt: If you have a job, are you safe from extreme poverty?
options: No — 284 million workers are still in extreme poverty
questions.whyCorrect: About 284 million people work and are still in extreme poverty — 7.9% of everyone with a job. Working hard and escaping poverty are not the same thing.
whyWrong: Millions of jobs don't pay enough to clear the line.
Plenty of full-time workers are still below the line.
questions.action: Look up the minimum wage where you live. Could you live on it?

questions.prompt: How many people have no social safety net at all — no benefits if they lose work or fall ill?
questions.whyCorrect: 3.8 billion people — close to half the planet. If their income stops, nothing catches them.
whyWrong: A hundred times too low.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Find out what would catch your family if income stopped.

questions.prompt: In what year did more than half the world finally have some kind of social safety net?
questions.whyCorrect: 2023 — the first time in history coverage passed 50%, at 52.4%. It was 42.8% as recently as 2015.
whyWrong: Coverage was a small fraction of the world then.
Still well under half.
questions.action: That happened in your lifetime. Ask what changed.

questions.prompt: About how many people live on less than $30 a day?
questions.whyCorrect: 6.7 billion — around 81% of everyone on Earth. Extreme poverty is the sharpest edge of a much bigger picture.
whyWrong: Far too low — most of the world is below this line.
That's the number below $3 a day, not $30.
questions.action: Work out your household's spending per person per day.

questions.prompt: Which group is most likely to be living in extreme poverty?
questions.whyCorrect: About 1 in 5 children are below the line, against 1 in 10 people overall — roughly double the risk. Around 412 million children live in extreme poverty.
whyWrong: Adults of working age have a lower poverty rate than children.
Older people face real risks, but children are the most affected group.
questions.action: Picture your class. One in five is the scale.

questions.prompt: Poverty isn't only about money. Which of these does the Multidimensional Poverty Index actually count?
options: How many holidays a family takes
Whether a home has clean cooking fuel
What brand of phone someone owns
questions.whyCorrect: Clean cooking fuel is a real poverty indicator. Cooking on open fires damages lungs and eats hours a day gathering fuel — usually done by women and girls who could be in school.
whyWrong: Holidays aren't measured — the MPI looks at basic survival needs.
Phone brand tells you nothing about whether a family can eat or wash.
questions.action: Find out what fuel cooked your dinner tonight.

questions.prompt: When you measure poverty by more than income, does the number of poor people go up or down?
questions.whyCorrect: It rises to 1.1 billion. Plenty of people scrape past $3 a day but still have no toilet, no electricity and children out of school — real poverty that a wage figure misses.
whyWrong: Counting more kinds of hardship finds more people, not fewer.
It's roughly 300 million higher than the income count.
questions.action: Name something you need for a good life that money alone doesn't show.

questions.prompt: Of the 1.1 billion people in multidimensional poverty, how many are children?
questions.whyCorrect: More than half. Poverty falls hardest on the people with the least power to do anything about it.
whyWrong: Far too low — it's over 50%.
Children are the single biggest group among the poor.
questions.action: Ask why poverty hits children hardest.

questions.prompt: In the world's poorest countries, roughly what share of people have any social safety net?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 9.7% — against 85.9% in rich countries. The places that need safety nets most are the ones least likely to have them.
whyWrong: That's the figure for high-income countries.
That's the global average, not the poorest countries.
questions.action: Compare 10% and 86%. Ask what causes that gap.

questions.prompt: Ending world hunger and poverty needs about $1.4 trillion a year. What share of poorer countries' economies is that?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 3.3% of their combined economies. The number sounds impossible until you see it as a share — then it becomes a choice rather than a physical limit.
whyWrong: Ten times too high. It's a small slice, not a third.
Nowhere near — no country could spend 80% on one thing.
questions.action: Look up what share of your country's budget goes to defence.

questions.prompt: Worldwide, what share of women hold official documents proving they own their land?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 24% of women hold legal land documents. Without paperwork, a woman can lose her home if she's widowed, divorced, or a relative makes a claim.
whyWrong: That's higher than the rate for the whole population (43%).
Far too high — most people worldwide have no formal documents.
questions.action: Find out whose name is on the paperwork where you live.

questions.prompt: How many people are poor AND live somewhere facing climate hazards like floods or drought?
questions.whyCorrect: 887 million — and 309 million of them face three or four hazards at once. Poverty and climate danger pile up in the same places.
whyWrong: This is the size of a small city.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Look up which climate hazards affect your area.

questions.prompt: If a family grows its own food, does that count when measuring whether they're poor?
options: Yes — food you grow counts as income
Only if they sell it at a market
questions.whyCorrect: Yes. Poverty measures count food a family grows for itself — otherwise farmers who eat well from their own land would look destitute on paper.
whyWrong: Counting only cash would badly misjudge millions of farming families.
It counts whether or not it's sold — what matters is that the family eats.
questions.action: Ask how you'd measure the wealth of a family that grows what it eats.

questions.prompt: The poverty line is $3 a day in every country. How can that be fair when prices differ?
options: It's adjusted so $3 buys the same amount everywhere
It isn't fair — it's the same cash amount
It only applies to people paid in dollars
questions.whyCorrect: The line is adjusted for local prices, so $3 buys roughly the same food and shelter in Malawi as in Mexico. Economists call it purchasing power parity.
whyWrong: That would make the line meaningless — $3 buys wildly different things in different countries.
It applies to everyone, whatever they're paid in.
questions.action: Compare the price of bread in two countries online.

questions.prompt: What does living below the extreme poverty line actually mean?
options: Not affording a tiny room, heating, and enough food to avoid malnutrition
questions.whyCorrect: The line is set exactly where a person can't afford a tiny space to live, minimum heating, and food that keeps them from becoming malnourished. It measures survival, not comfort.
whyWrong: Lots of people who aren't poor don't own cars.
Missing a holiday isn't poverty — this line is about staying alive and fed.
questions.action: Notice how often 'poor' gets used for things that aren't poverty.

questions.prompt: Which region has the largest share of its people living in extreme poverty?
questions.whyCorrect: Sub-Saharan Africa, where nearly 40% of people live in extreme poverty — the highest rate of any region.
whyWrong: Western Europe has some of the strongest safety nets in the world.
North America has poverty, but nothing on this scale.
questions.action: Find Sub-Saharan Africa on a map and name three countries in it.

questions.prompt: COVID-19 pushed roughly how many extra people into extreme poverty?
questions.whyCorrect: About 50 million — the first big rise in a generation. Decades of steady progress can be knocked back by a single event.
whyWrong: A thousand times too low.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Ask what helped some families survive the pandemic and not others.

questions.prompt: The world's goal is to end extreme poverty by 2030. Are we on track?
options: No — about 9% will still be in extreme poverty
Yes, and it will be done early
questions.whyCorrect: At the current pace about 9% of the world — hundreds of millions of people — will still be in extreme poverty in 2030. The target will be missed.
whyWrong: Poverty reduction has stalled, not accelerated.
Progress has slowed sharply since 2020.
questions.action: Name one thing that would speed this up.

questions.prompt: How many children have no social protection — no safety net at all?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.4 billion children. More than one in every two children alive has nothing to catch them if their family's income disappears.
whyWrong: A thousand times too low.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Find out if your country pays any kind of child benefit.

questions.prompt: About what share of the world lives on less than $10 a day?
questions.whyCorrect: About 52% — more than half the world. Clearing the extreme poverty line is a long way from being comfortable.
whyWrong: That's roughly the share below $3 a day.
Too high — 81% live below $30 a day, but $10 is about half.
questions.action: Work out what $10 a day would cover where you live.

questions.prompt: Are men or women more likely to have social protection?
questions.whyCorrect: Men, at 54.6% against 50.1% for women. Many benefits are linked to formal paid jobs — and women do far more unpaid and informal work.
whyWrong: It runs the other way: women are the less-covered group.
There's a gap of about 4.5 percentage points.
questions.action: List the unpaid work done in your home this week, and by whom.

questions.prompt: In the world's least developed countries, about what share of working people are still in extreme poverty?
questions.whyCorrect: About 30% — nearly one in three workers. Globally it's 6.9%, so where you're born makes an enormous difference to whether work pays enough to live on.
whyWrong: Too high — though it shows how severe the problem is that this seems believable.
That's below even the global average.
questions.action: Compare the minimum wage in two countries on different continents.

questions.prompt: The Multidimensional Poverty Index measures three things. Which set is it?
questions.whyCorrect: Health, education and living standards — measured through 10 indicators like nutrition, school attendance, clean water and electricity.
whyWrong: These are all money measures, and the whole point of the MPI is to look past money.
These are economic measures, not the three dimensions of poverty.
questions.action: Pick which of the three you'd fix first, and say why.

questions.prompt: Many people feel their land is theirs. But what share actually hold official documents proving it?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 43% hold documents, though 66% feel secure. That gap matters — without paperwork, families can be moved off land they've farmed for generations.
whyWrong: That's the share who *feel* secure, not who can prove it.
Far too high — most people worldwide have no formal land documents.
questions.action: Ask what proves who owns a home where you live.

questions.prompt: Extreme poverty is becoming concentrated in which kinds of places?
options: Countries affected by war and conflict
questions.whyCorrect: Conflict-affected and fragile places. War destroys the schools, clinics, markets and records that people need to escape poverty — so it's hardest to shift there.
whyWrong: Cities have poverty, but conflict is the defining pattern.
Tourist regions aren't where extreme poverty concentrates.
questions.action: Look up one country where conflict reversed progress on poverty.

questions.prompt: Rich countries spend about 60% of their budgets on essential services like health and schools. What do developing countries spend?
questions.whyCorrect: About 43%. The countries with the greatest needs have both smaller budgets and a smaller share of them going to the services that reduce poverty.
whyWrong: They spend a smaller share than rich countries, not a larger one.
Nowhere near — debt and other costs take much of their budgets.
questions.action: Look up what share of your country's budget goes to health and schools.

questions.prompt: How many poor people face three or four different climate hazards at the same time?
questions.whyCorrect: 309 million people face drought and flood and heat, stacked on top of each other. Recovering from one disaster is hard; recovering from several at once is close to impossible.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Name three hazards that could hit one place in a single year.

questions.prompt: What has been happening recently to international aid for fighting poverty?
options: It has fallen back to 2015 levels
questions.whyCorrect: It has dropped sharply, back to where it was in 2015 — at exactly the moment progress on poverty has stalled and needs are rising.
whyWrong: It has fallen, not risen.
There's been a sharp decline.
questions.action: Look up whether your country's aid budget rose or fell last year.

questions.prompt: In Sub-Saharan Africa, what share of people hold formal documents for their land?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 15%. Land is often a family's single biggest asset, and most people there have no paper proof that it's theirs.
whyWrong: Far too high for any world region.
That's closer to the global average of 43%.
questions.action: Ask what happens in a land dispute when nobody has documents.

questions.prompt: About how many children live in households below the extreme poverty line?
questions.whyCorrect: About 412 million children — roughly 1 in 5 children on Earth.
whyWrong: A hundred times too low.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Count to five. That ratio is the scale of child poverty.

questions.prompt: Has working poverty — people who work but stay poor — got better or worse since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: It improved, from 8.4% to 6.9%. Real progress — and it still leaves over 240 million workers in extreme poverty.
whyWrong: It moved the other way — this is good news.
There was a clear improvement of about 1.5 percentage points.
questions.action: Practise saying a fact that's good news and bad news at once.

questions.prompt: In 1990, about how many people lived in extreme poverty?
questions.whyCorrect: About 2.3 billion — roughly 44% of everyone alive at the time. Nearly three times today's number.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Too high — it was under half the world, not most of it.
questions.action: Ask an adult what they remember about the world in 1990.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many people worldwide live in extreme poverty right now?
questions.whyCorrect: About 800 million — roughly 1 in 10 people. Different agencies publish 808, 826 or 831 million depending on when they measured.
whyWrong: A hundred times too low.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: In a crowd of 30 people, that's 3 of them.

questions.prompt: The MPI counts a family as poor if they lack basics. Which of these counts as a deprivation?
questions.whyCorrect: No electricity is a real deprivation — it means no light to study by, no way to refrigerate food or medicine, no charging a phone to find work.
whyWrong: A garden isn't one of the ten indicators.
Televisions aren't a measure of poverty.
questions.action: List everything you did today that needed electricity.

questions.prompt: Why does Goal 1 include a target about surviving disasters and economic shocks?
options: Because disasters only happen in rich countries
Because disasters have nothing to do with poverty
Because one flood or lost job can push a family straight back into poverty
questions.whyCorrect: A family can climb out of poverty over years and be knocked back by a single flood, drought or lost job. Staying out is as hard as getting out.
whyWrong: Poorer places are hit hardest and take longest to recover.
887 million poor people live in areas facing climate hazards.
questions.action: Ask what would happen if your household's income stopped for three months.

questions.prompt: Poverty halved in 136 years, then halved again in 45, then again in 13. What does that show?
questions.whyCorrect: Progress accelerated dramatically as health, schooling and industry spread. But it has stalled since 2020 — speeding up isn't guaranteed to continue.
whyWrong: Each halving took less time than the one before.
The rate of change transformed completely.
questions.action: Sketch those three numbers on a timeline.

questions.prompt: How many people are multidimensionally poor — lacking things like clean water, schooling or electricity?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.1 billion people across 109 countries — about 17% of everyone surveyed, and more than the number counted by income alone.
whyWrong: A hundred times too low.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Notice this is bigger than the income count. Ask why.

questions.prompt: Why is gathering cooking fuel treated as a poverty problem?
options: It's only a problem for farmers
It takes hours a day and the smoke damages lungs
questions.whyCorrect: Hours spent collecting firewood are hours not spent in school or earning. And cooking over open fires causes serious lung disease, mostly in women and children.
whyWrong: It affects households in towns and villages alike.
It's about health and lost time, not flavour.
questions.action: Work out how many hours a week you'd lose gathering fuel.

questions.prompt: The poverty line used to be $1.90 a day and is now $3.00. Why did it change?
options: Poverty got worse so they raised it
Prices rose, so the line was updated to mean the same hardship
questions.whyCorrect: $1.90 in 2011 prices and $3.00 in 2021 prices buy about the same amount. The number moved because money changed value, not because the standard did.
whyWrong: The line tracks prices, not the poverty rate.
It's set from detailed price surveys across many countries.
questions.action: Ask an adult what a chocolate bar cost when they were your age.

questions.prompt: One of Goal 1's targets is social protection for everyone. How far off is that?
questions.whyCorrect: Just over half — 52.4%. It's the first time in history coverage passed 50%, and it still leaves 3.8 billion people with nothing.
whyWrong: Nearly half the world has no coverage at all.
Far from it — this is one of the least-completed targets.
questions.action: Find out what benefits exist where you live, and who misses out.

questions.prompt: About how many workers worldwide earn too little to escape extreme poverty?
questions.whyCorrect: Over 240 million workers. They have jobs, they work full days, and it still isn't enough to clear the line.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
Too high — that would be most of the world's workers.
questions.action: Ask what makes the difference between a job and a living.

questions.prompt: About 740 million poor people live in middle-income countries. What does that tell you?
options: A country can be doing well on average while millions inside it are poor
Middle-income countries are the poorest on Earth
Averages always tell the full story
questions.whyCorrect: National averages hide who's being left behind. A country's economy can grow while huge numbers of its people see none of it — which is why inequality matters as much as growth.
whyWrong: They're not the poorest — they're simply where most poor people live.
This is exactly the case where an average misleads you.
questions.action: Find one statistic about your country and ask who it hides.

questions.prompt: What fraction of the world lives in extreme poverty today?
questions.whyCorrect: About 1 in 10 — roughly 9 to 10% of everyone alive. Two hundred years ago it was 3 in 4.
whyWrong: Ten times too optimistic.
That was roughly true in the 1950s.
questions.action: Compare 1 in 10 today with 3 in 4 in 1820.

questions.prompt: What is the single biggest thing that would help end extreme poverty?
options: A mix of decent pay, safety nets and basic services
Waiting for it to fix itself
questions.whyCorrect: No single fix works. 284 million people work and stay poor, 3.8 billion have no safety net, and 1.1 billion lack basics like water and electricity — so it takes pay, protection and services together.
whyWrong: Progress has stalled since 2020 — it doesn't happen on its own.
Food matters in an emergency, but it doesn't fix why a family had none.
questions.action: Pick the one you'd fund first and defend your choice.
